title: Vitamin D Deficiency in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Low vitamin D leads to hypocalcaemia, rickets and osteomalacia. In East Africa, sun exposure, diet, HIV and TB therapy are key causes. Diagnosis relies on low 25(OH)D, low phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase.

sections.p: Vitamin D deficiency is defined by serum 25‑hydroxyvitamin D <20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L). In children it presents with bone pain, growth faltering and hypocalcaemia.

t.b: Is the best marker of vitamin D status? A low level confirms deficiency.
Shows hypocalcaemia; low ionised Ca²⁺ is most relevant.
Low phosphate supports vitamin D deficiency over hypoparathyroidism.
Raised levels indicate increased bone turnover, common in rickets.

sections.p: Severity is staged by biochemical and clinical features.
b: Moderate: 5–10 ng/mL, bone pain, growth delay
Severe: <5 ng/mL, rickets, fractures, hypocalcaemic seizures

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the leading causes are sun‑protection habits, dark skin, exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, HIV/TB therapy and malabsorption.
b: Exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D drops

sections.p: Children may have bone pain, delayed milestones, waddling gait, and in severe cases, hypocalcaemic seizures.
b: Bone pain, especially in legs and back

sections.p: Basic tests are often available; use them to confirm and rule out mimics.

t.b: Detects hypocalcaemia; ionised is most accurate.
Low in vitamin D deficiency; normal or high in hypoparathyroidism.
Elevated in secondary hyperparathyroidism; normal in primary deficiency.

sections.p: Severe deficiency can cause life‑threatening hypocalcaemia and cardiac arrhythmia.
Treat the underlying cause, replace vitamin D and calcium, and monitor biochemical response.
b: Address malabsorption (e.g., treat TB, give fat‑soluble vitamins)

t.b: Why high dose? To rapidly restore stores; maintenance keeps levels >30 ng/mL.
Why? To correct hypocalcaemia and support bone mineralisation.
Why? It induces CYP450, increasing vitamin D catabolism.

sections.p: Re‑check 25(OH)D after 3–6 months and monitor growth.
Other causes of hypocalcaemia and rickets.
b: Malnutrition without vitamin D – calcium low

sections.p: Total calcium can be normal if albumin is low; ionised calcium is more reliable.
b: PTH can be normal in early deficiency; repeat if clinical suspicion high

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained bone fractures in a child

faq.q: Why is vitamin D important for bone health?
faq.a: It promotes intestinal calcium absorption and bone mineralisation.

faq.q: Can a child with rickets develop heart problems?
faq.a: Yes, severe hypocalcaemia can prolong QT and cause arrhythmias.

faq.q: What if a child is on antiepileptics?
faq.a: Enzyme inducers increase vitamin D breakdown; give higher doses or switch drugs.

exam: A 2‑year‑old boy presents with bowed legs and delayed milestones. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency; look for low 25(OH)D, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase.
A child on phenobarbital develops hypocalcaemic seizures. What is the best next step? — Stop or switch the enzyme inducer; give high‑dose vitamin D and calcium.
A 5‑year‑old with HIV on rifampicin has low calcium. Which vitamin is most likely deficient? — Vitamin D; rifampicin induces its metabolism.
You suspect rickets but the alkaline phosphatase is normal. What could explain this? — Early disease, or laboratory error; repeat test or assess clinical signs.
A child has low calcium but normal phosphate. Which condition is least likely? — Vitamin D deficiency (would have low phosphate).
A patient with hypocalcaemia has a normal PTH. What does this suggest? — Primary hypoparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency; further tests needed.
